extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, agency officials, policymakers, and regulatory reformers
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating how notice-and-comment (including e-rulemaking) procedures should be designed and interpreted so agency decisionmaking is democratically responsive; includes criteria for when and how agencies should treat mass or value-laden public comments. Targeted at law/policy analysis and agency practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: E-rulemaking expands public participation and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: E-rulemaking is the use of technology to: (i) help develop proposed rules; (ii) make rulemaking materials broadly available online; and (iii) enable more effective and diverse public participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E-rulemaking can permit the public to more readily view the identity of commenters and the content of comments, and may 'enlarge significantly a genuine public sphere' and foster greater public involvement; however usability, transparency, and accessibility of e-dockets must be addressed (e.g., posting significant materials and comments so the e-dockets are authoritative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 553 procedural requirements (notice, comment, concise statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under APA §553 an agency must provide public notice of a proposed rule and a 'concise general statement of . . . basis and purpose.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial gloss requires agencies publicly disclose the data on which they rely prior to seeking comment and to explain reasons for rejecting significant comments; these procedures are a key source of accountability and democratic responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond substantively to significant comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency must respond to the substance of significant comments received during rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of judicial interpretation (e.g., Nova Scotia Food Prods.), agencies are expected to answer significant comments in the final rule explanation; failure to do so risks vacatur as arbitrary and capricious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid arbitrary and capricious decisionmaking; provide reasoned explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial review can vacate an agency decision if it is not reasoned, does not follow substantive legal requirements, or is arbitrary or capricious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should disclose and justify actions in light of statutory constraints; courts enforce procedural requirements and review for essential reasonableness under the APA.

rubrics_metrics.name: When multiple value-laden comments deserve especial attention (five-part test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies might consider the following criteria for deciding when multiple value-laden comments deserve especial attention: (1) comments submitted are particularly numerous, (2) a particular viewpoint represents a strong majority or a supermajority of the comments filed, (3) the comments raise an issue relevant under the agency’s statutory authorization, (4) the comments are coherent and persuasive, and (5) the comments point in a different direction from that considered by the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially where comments point in a direction different from the agency's proposed path, they can signal the need for further investigation or deliberation (e.g., targeted polling, focus groups, or elevating the issue within the executive branch).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat comments as dispositive votes; treat mass comments as signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies ought not formalistically treat public comments as a dispositive 'vote.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than adding up comments to determine rule outcome, agencies should consider whether mass or value-laden commenting signals a need for deeper inquiry, additional procedures, or deliberation; comments can be a 'rough cut' at public views prompting further engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate form-letter or identical-text campaigns appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of identical or near-identical text in a comment may imply the comment does not convey a uniquely held view, but it does not make the comment content-free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should recognize that portals lower participation costs and that form letters often reflect real preferences; but treat such comments carefully—consider representativeness, attribution, and whether commenters individualized text when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider representativeness and limits of mass commenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass comment campaigns may not be representative of the public at large and may reflect particular interest group memberships or internet access disparities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should weigh representativeness concerns and the underrepresentation of diffuse beneficiary groups, but not ignore extensive participation; consider complementary methods (randomized polls, focus groups) to probe intensity and breadth of views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use focused questions in notices to elicit higher-quality lay input
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies could reshape their notices by more often using focused questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focused questions tend to produce more valuable lay reactions on core values and prioritization than open-ended notices; agencies already sometimes use this technique (e.g., Department of Transportation listening sessions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM) to solicit values early
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should be encouraged to use the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking process to solicit value preferences prior to embarking on a more specific rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Soliciting values earlier can avoid the 'fait accompli' effect at proposed-rule stage and improve deliberation over value-laden choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplement public comments with additional deliberative methods
rubrics_metrics.description: When public comments indicate unexpected or significant public views, agencies might conduct targeted opinion polling, focus groups, randomly selected citizen juries, or elevate the issue within the executive branch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each method has tradeoffs (e.g., small size of juries/focus groups), but these techniques can confirm presence and intensity of public views and should be summarized in the final rule if used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide guidance to the public on what makes a higher-quality comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies could regularly provide information to the public on what makes for a higher quality, more persuasive comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance helps improve the usefulness of lay and value-focused commenting and can reduce low-value submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize astroturfing and manage anonymous/comment attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies might require an affirmation that the commenter has not been paid and announce that anonymous comments will receive less weight; offer redaction on request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These steps can reduce manipulation by interest groups; barring anonymous comments could be coupled with redaction options when privacy is a concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make e-dockets complete and authoritative; post significant materials and comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Some agencies are failing to post many significant rulemaking materials—including submitted comments—so the publicly accessible portion of the database is not complete and e-dockets are not authoritative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For e-rulemaking to realize its promise, agencies should post data relied on prior to comment, post submitted comments, and ensure the e-docket is an authoritative public record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about executive branch review and influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Information regarding the content of executive branch changes to agency rules is often extraordinarily limited; Presidents may try to maintain deniability regarding agency action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of transparency about presidential or White House supervision impairs accountability; agencies and the executive should disclose content of supervision/changes to permit electoral and public accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-regulation via internal commitments to consider lay comments
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of specific congressional instructions, executive branch entities could, by internal agency rule, guidance, or executive order, commit to weigh layperson comments in a particular way or to conduct additional proceedings if lay comments suggest public opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-regulation coupled with transparency (summaries in final rules and explanation of weight given) can provide incentives for agencies to be democratically responsive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit judicial review to acknowledgement and explanation, not mandated weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should require agencies to give some acknowledgement of significant views expressed through lay comments, and then defer to the agency's subsequent response rather than mandate particular weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring courts to determine 'adequate weight' for value-laden comments risks judges imposing personal values; courts should instead ensure transparency and reasoned engagement with significant comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulemaking procedures as a source of democratic responsiveness (pluralist and civic republican dimensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency procedures can contribute to democratic legitimacy either by enabling input from a wide variety of interests (pluralist) or by facilitating democratic deliberation (civic republican).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under a pluralist view, mechanisms that allow broad participation and standing help aggregate interests; under a civic republican view, mechanisms that promote deliberation (opportunity to be heard, agency explanation, exchange of reasons) are central—e-rulemaking improvements and procedural experimentation should aim to serve one or both functions.
